title: We love because (1 John 4:19–21)
hook: we love him because he first loved us

segments.voice: Yesterday, perfect love casts out fear, and your line was no fear in love. What did you do from love that fear had been holding back? Day six hundred ninety-one.

Stand at the edge of a canyon and say nothing, and the canyon says nothing back. Call out, and a moment later the rock answers in your own voice. An echo never goes first. It only exists because something reached it. Yesterday the letter said that love throws out fear. Today the writer asks where that love comes from in the first place. The passage is three verses long, and its first line is about exactly that: which love comes first, and which one answers.

In the King James Bible: "We love him, because he first loved us." Short enough to carry, and some readers hear the whole letter in it. In the writer's telling, our love is a response, and God's love goes first. Some readers also notice that the line still stands without the word him: we love, because he first loved us. Read that way, it isn't only, we love God because God loved us. It's, we love at all, anyone at all, because we were loved first. On that reading, every kind of love, for God and for neighbor, has the same source. Then the writer makes it very concrete, and very uncomfortable: "If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" He's not being harsh for the fun of it. He's pointing out something simple. God is invisible. Your brother is right in front of you, with all his irritating habits. If you can't love the one you can see, the claim to love the one you can't is hard to believe. It's a test anyone can turn on themselves, and the letter doesn't pretend anyone passes it cleanly. That may be why the test comes right after the line about who loved first. And then the last line of this section: "And this commandment have we from him, That he who loveth God love his brother also." One commandment, pointing two ways: up toward the God no one has seen, and sideways toward the brother in the next chair. The letter has been circling this from its first page. Light, children, deeds, fear. Here it lands: we love, because he first loved us.
screen: then, large: `BECAUSE HE FIRST LOVED US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive love before giving it. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to love anyone for a minute. Instead, remember being loved. A parent's voice. A friend who stayed. A teacher who believed you could. A stranger's kindness on a bad day. Let one memory come, and stay in it. Let yourself be on the receiving end, without hurrying to pay it back. Notice where you feel it in your body. If you pray, you can receive God's love the same way, with nothing to do but be loved. Then, only at the end, notice whether anything in you wants to answer. The bell holds the time.
Echo. The hook's picture for our love: it never goes first, First John says, because he first loved us, and we only answer back.
Your line: he first loved us. Today, thank one person who loved you first, before you'd done anything to earn it. Day six hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: 1 John 4:19 is a short verse some Christians memorize as a summary of their faith, and some churches teach it to children.

original.note: Greek: first. the word behind 'he first loved us'.

what it means: all our love, for God and neighbor, is an answer to a love that came first.
what a scholar hears: prōtos, first; a verse that can be heard with no object at all, as the source of every love; and a test that ties the seen brother to the unseen God.

notes: Textual note: the earliest manuscripts (e.g. Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) read ἡμεῖς ἀγαπῶμεν without an object; later manuscripts add αὐτόν ('him') or τὸν θεόν. Confirm.
'πρῶτος' in 4:19 (ὅτι αὐτὸς πρῶτος ἠγάπησεν ἡμᾶς): confirm. The 'prototype' etymology was cut in review.
howItsDone's baptism and wedding claims were cut in review.

Softened 'the oldest manuscripts' to 'some of the oldest': Sinaiticus, also very early, reads 'we love God' (τὸν θεόν). The wider reading (love of anyone, not only of God) is interpretive and framed as 'read that way'.

Editor review (2026-10-01): under the claims rule, the manuscript claim (no 'him' in some early copies) was cut from the teach, screen, match, myth and trapdoor and reframed as 'some readers notice the line stands without him'; a Keeper may restore it with a cited source. New canyon-echo hook replaces the baby's smile (too close to day 690's toddler). Cut 'one of the shortest of our readings', 'four chapters', 'nobody passes it perfectly... that's why it matters' (narrator theology), the 'prototype' etymology and the howItsDone baptism/wedding claims; replaced the 'two commandments' myth, which repeated day 687's 'one commandment' item.
